claim: NLI-based semantic entropy/semantic sets, the standard sampling-based UQ method transferred from NLG, performs near chance for code correctness prediction because NLI models cannot distinguish functionally different code and collapse nearly all sampled responses into a single cluster.
stance_target: expressed/proxy uncertainty interfaces for code fail to communicate a real internal signal even when repeated sampling is used, unless the equivalence check is made execution-aware
scope_conditions: 5 closed-API LLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-2.5-Pro/Flash/Flash-Lite); LiveCodeBench (Python), MultiPL-E (Java), LiveSQLBench (SQL); m=10 samples, temperature 1.0
quoted_support: NLI-based semantic entropy and semantic sets confidence perform near chance across all three languages, ranging from 0.47-0.58 on SQL, 0.48-0.56 on Java, and 0.50-0.53 on Python... a consequence of NLI models assigning nearly all responses to a single cluster regardless of functional differences.

claim: Replacing NLI-based semantic equivalence with an LLM-judge functional-equivalence assessment (does code produce identical outputs for all valid inputs) recovers strong discrimination, achieving top AUROC in 11 of 15 model-benchmark combinations.
stance_target: whether the internal sampling-confidence signal can be made usable via better clustering rather than a lightweight expressed interface
scope_conditions: Same 5-model, 3-language, 1711-problem setup; judge model Gemini-2.5-Flash validated at 93-97% precision vs execution ground truth
quoted_support: Functional equivalence methods achieve top AUROC in 11 out of 15 model-benchmark combinations and the best calibration across most settings, consistently outperforming both NLI-based counterparts and all other methods evaluated.
numbers: AUROC up to 0.84 (SQL, GPT-4o-mini functional sets)

claim: Verbalized confidence performance is inconsistent across models and languages, ranging from near-chance to moderately good, echoing the fragility of verbal self-report as a confidence interface.
stance_target: verbalized confidence fails to reliably communicate correctness likelihood in code generation
scope_conditions: 6-level Likert verbalized confidence prompt, 5 closed-API LLMs, 3 languages
quoted_support: verbalized confidence is inconsistent (0.60–0.80)... verbalized confidence shows inconsistent results, ranging from 0.54 on Gemini-2.5-Flash to 0.74 on Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite.

claim: The study explicitly excludes open-weight models (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek) and states results should not be assumed to transfer to them, leaving a direct gap for open-weight single-GPU studies.
stance_target: generalizability of functional-equivalence UQ findings to open-weight 7B code models
scope_conditions: Model coverage limitation, stated by authors
quoted_support: All five models evaluated are closed-source API models from two providers (OpenAI and Google)... our evaluation does not include open-weight models (e.g., Llama, Mistral, Qwen), which are increasingly common in cost-sensitive deployment settings. Our results should not be assumed to transfer directly to these or other LLMs without further evaluation.

claim: Sampling-based consistency can rank correct vs. incorrect generations effectively even for weak models with very low accuracy, e.g. GPT-4o-mini reaches 0.84 AUROC with functional entropy on SQL despite 0.21 pass@1 accuracy.
stance_target: sampling-based/consistency confidence signals remain discriminative independent of base model accuracy, consistent with the paper's near-perfect internal-calibration finding
quoted_support: Notably, on SQL, GPT-4o-mini achieves 0.84 AUROC with functional entropy despite having the lowest accuracy (0.21), illustrating that sampling-based consistency can rank correct and incorrect generations effectively even for weak models.

claim: m=5 sampled generations captures most of the AUROC gain of functional equivalence methods (within 0.01-0.02 of m=10), suggesting the resampling cost required for a strong internal signal can be reduced without much loss.
stance_target: compute feasibility of sampling-confidence methods on single-GPU budgets
scope_conditions: Ablation across benchmarks and models, Appendix F.1
quoted_support: our ablation in Appendix F.1 shows that m=5 captures most of the AUROC gain (within 0.01–0.02 of m=10 across most settings), reducing functional equivalence rate to 5 judge calls per prompt and clustering-based methods to at most 15.
